By Rosanne Villalobos
THISTLETON (6 February)—Larchmere Print and Packaging will move its operations to a larger site north of town, the firm confirmed this week. Its Wesley Street premises can no longer hold the presses needed to meet rising orders for folded cartons. The new building at Hollowbrook Industrial Park offers 4,200 square meters, nearly twice the present production area.
"We have been turning work away for want of room for a fourth press," said Ingrid Solberg, the operations manager. "How orders are taken and handled will not alter, and no counter post will be lost."
The handover will proceed in three stages. In the first, beginning on 2 March, contractors will fit out the new building. In the second, from 20 April, company engineers will move the presses across, and although production will pause briefly, no order deadline will be affected. In the third, beginning on 1 June, the order collection point will transfer to Hollowbrook.
Ordering by telephone or through the online portal remains unchanged, as do current prices and counter opening hours. The one difference for customers is that from the third stage, finished work must be collected at Hollowbrook rather than on Wesley Street. The firm also plans to hire 12 production staff. Applications close on 21 February and should be sent to its personnel office.

HARTWELL (12 September)— The Hartwell Growers' Market is opening a second trading location to keep up with rising demand. — [1] —. Over the past year, the Saturday market has welcomed an average of more than 4,000 shoppers each week, roughly double the number recorded two years earlier.
The market has operated on Meadow Street for eight years, where 25 stalls sell fresh produce, baked goods, and crafts every Saturday morning. Organizers say the growth is largely the result of several new farms joining from the surrounding valley, which has widened the range of goods on offer and drawn visitors from neighboring towns.
To ease the crowding, a second market will open at Cranford Square, close to the town's central bus stop. — [2] —. The new site will run on Wednesdays and Thursdays from 9 a.m. to 3 p.m., with room for up to 40 stalls, and sellers will pay a rental fee of 20 dollars per day.
"The weekday market means that people who work on weekends can finally buy fresh vegetables and bread from local producers," said Beatrice Nolan, director of the Hartwell Community Market Association. — [3] —. Samuel Ortega, who sells honey and preserves at the Meadow Street site, added that the extra days would help him reach customers he had never met before.
The association hopes to add a covered seating area for the colder months and is already considering a third location on the eastern edge of town. — [4] —.

Thornhedge Nursery Welcomes Visitors to Its Second Store
ARDENFORD (14 March) - Thornhedge Nursery, a family-run garden business known across the region for its wide selection of shrubs and flowering plants, has opened a second store on Wexley Lane in Ardenford.
The business began eleven years ago as a single stall selling potted herbs at a weekend market. Yvonne Castellan, who started Thornhedge and continues to oversee its day-to-day operations, said the company's steady growth had come from modest beginnings. "We had only a small table and a few dozen plants when we opened," she
recalled
. "Every step since then has been guided by what our customers ask us for, and this new store is the clearest sign yet of how far that has taken us."
The Ardenford store occupies a converted warehouse and features a bright indoor display hall, a covered courtyard for larger trees, and a separate room set aside for teaching. Wide aisles allow visitors to move easily between the seasonal arrangements, and a central advice counter is staffed throughout the day so that shoppers can ask about plant care before they buy.
The new location also introduces a program of hands-on planting workshops, something the first store was never able to accommodate. Sessions are held twice each week, and each one is limited to sixteen participants so that staff can give individual attention. Topics range from container gardening to the care of indoor foliage.
The store is open every day except Tuesday, from nine in the morning until six in the evening. General entry carries no charge, and throughout the opening month the nursery is offering each visitor a complimentary young seedling to take home.
"A garden center should be a place where people feel welcome to learn, not only to buy," Ms. Castellan said. "I hope this store gives our neighbours somewhere to spend an afternoon and to leave with something they have grown themselves."

September 20 — For more than forty years, Foxglove Craft Supply has sold yarn, paint, clay, and countless other materials to the makers of Denbury. In all that time, however, the shop has never once offered guided classes of its own. That is about to change. Beginning next month, the store will run The Maker Sessions, a series of hands-on workshops in which shoppers can learn a new craft from start to finish and walk out with something they have made themselves.
Delia Faust, who manages events at the store, said the idea came from customers themselves. "People buy the supplies and then tell us they are not quite sure where to begin," she said. "We wanted to give them a place to sit down, try something, and leave with a finished piece they made by hand."
To introduce the program, Foxglove will hold a free taster afternoon on Saturday, October 5, when visitors can watch short demonstrations and ask questions at no cost. The paid sessions themselves begin on Saturday, October 19. Places are limited, and customers are encouraged to reserve a spot in advance, either through the store's Web page or at the customer desk.

To: All Members
From: Louise Trevino
Date: 4 March
Subject: March skills workshop

Dear Members,

The Cadwell Business Association is pleased to invite you to our next member skills workshop, to be held at 6:30 P.M. on Thursday, 20 March, in the Marrick Conference Room at our main office. The session is free for all members, and no prior preparation is required.

What to expect:
- A ninety-minute session on planning and managing daily operations
- A guided exercise based on real workplace examples
- A question-and-answer period with the presenter
- A printed planning toolkit for every participant to take home

This month's session will be led by Desmond Attah, who served as operations director for eighteen years at Hartigan and Vale. Alongside that work, he co-runs a small print shop with his sister, and he gives three hours each week to the Bright Futures Coding Club.

To reserve a place, please reply to this message no later than Monday, 17 March, so that we can confirm seating.

Kind regards,
Louise Trevino
----------------------
http://www.summitskills.co - Meet Our Presenters

Interviewer: Welcome, Desmond. Could you tell our members a little about your professional background?

Desmond Attah: Of course. I spent nearly two decades as an operations director at a commercial insurance provider, where I was responsible for coordinating the daily workflow across several busy departments.

Interviewer: And where did your training begin?

Desmond Attah: I completed a diploma in business administration at the Corley Institute, which gave me a solid foundation long before I ever managed a team.

Interviewer: What will you focus on in your workshop for members?

Desmond Attah: I will show participants simple, practical ways to plan their working day and keep projects on schedule, all without relying on extra software.
----------------------
**Bright Futures Coding Club**

Do you know a young person who is eager to learn how technology really works? Join a growing program that helps them build genuine skills, one session at a time.

How it works:
- Open to students between the ages of 11 and 16
- No experience or equipment required
- Every student is paired with a friendly mentor
- Places are offered on a first-come basis

Sessions run every Saturday morning throughout the school term.

Last year we welcomed more than 300 young people to our sessions.

The Bright Futures Coding Club is run entirely by volunteers, and our aim is simple: to help young people in our community gain practical coding skills that open doors to future study and work.

To take part, or to offer your time as a mentor, sign up at www.brightfuturesclub.org.

From: Harriet Voss, Membership Coordinator
To: Trevor Aldington
Subject: Welcome to the Fernbrook Tool Library
Date: 12 March
Dear Mr. Aldington,
Thank you for joining the Fernbrook Tool Library, a member-supported service that lends everyday equipment such as power drills, extension ladders, garden tools, and floor-cleaning machines. The library operates from a small workshop on Halbern Row in the Wexford district, and members may reserve items online at any time. Below are the main rules that apply to every reservation.
1. Each item may be borrowed for a maximum of fourteen days before it must be returned or renewed.
2. A refundable deposit equal to twenty percent of an item's replacement value is held for the length of the loan.
3. Items returned after the due date are subject to an overdue charge of two dollars per item per day.
4. Reservations covering fewer than three days must be approved in advance by a staff coordinator, as short loans require additional handling.
5. Members in good standing may borrow up to five items at one time at no additional charge.
6. All members receive one free equipment-safety workshop each year.
If you intend to collect your items outside our staffed opening hours, please make sure you have activated your locker access code before arriving, as our counter staff will not be present to assist you.
Kind regards,
Harriet Voss
